To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the risk of atherothrombotic events (including myocardial infarct) is increased in patients with HIV infection; (2) this increased risk is largely explained by the presence of traditional cardiovascular disease risk factors, such as smoking, diabetes, and hypertension; and (3) the risk of death from atherothrombosis is significantly reduced by antiretrovial therapy, particularly when it includes a protease inhibitor.
In a large prospective study of HIV-infected adults, antiretrovirus therapy (ART) was associated with a significantly reduced risk of atherosclerosis and death from other non-cardiovascular causes.
the risk of AtD is low and is not increased by PI-containing regimens in the short-term follow-up of our study.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the risks and benefits of antiretrovial therapy (ART) on cardiovascular disease in HIV-infected patients.
the risks of cardiovascular disease associated with HIV infection.
the risk of atherothrombotic disease (AtD), including myocardial infarct (MI), stroke and peripheral vascular disease (PVD), in HIV-infected individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of AtD associated with the use PI-based regimens is low, but not negligible.
the use of ART in general and of PIs in particular does not increase the risk of atherothrombotic events.
the risk of atherogenesis is not increased by antiretrovials, but the risk of death is reduced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that there are significant benefits of antiretrovirus therapy in reducing mortality and that the risk of atherothrombotic events is low in the short term.
HIV-infected persons are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease and this increased risk is not completely explained by traditional risk factors.
HIV-infected patients should receive antiretrovials and should be encouraged to stop smoking, control their blood pressure, and control their blood sugar.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the benefits of ART in reducing mortality outweigh any risks of atherosclerosis in the short-term.
the risk of a cardiovascular event in patients receiving ART is low.
the risk of myocardial events is not increased in the short-term by the use of protease inhibitor therapy.
